passages.t: Who may eat the holy food
passages.happening:
“Tell Aaron and his sons to treat with respect the sacred offerings that the Israelites have consecrated to Me, so that they do not profane My holy name” (verse 2).

A priest who is unclean, from a skin disease, a discharge or touching something dead, may not eat the sacred offerings until he is clean (verses 3-6). “When the sun has set, he will become clean, and then he may eat from the sacred offerings, for they are his food” (verse 7).

No one outside the priest's household may eat them. A guest or a hired worker may not. A slave of the household may (verses 10-11). A priest's daughter who marries outside the priesthood no longer eats them; but if she is widowed or divorced, has no children and comes home, “she may share her father’s food as in her youth” (verse 13). Someone who eats by mistake repays the value and adds a fifth (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The priests had no farmland. They lived on their share of the offerings and on tithes. The holy food was their household's daily bread, so the question of who could eat it was a question about family life.

Two simple rules govern it.

The eater must be clean. Uncleanness was a normal part of life, for priests as for anyone, and it was not sin. An unclean priest simply waited until evening, washed, and then ate. Verse 7 is gentle: the offerings ‘are his food’. He is not kept from them long.

And the eater must belong to the house. The lines follow the household of that world. A slave bought by the priest or born under his roof was part of the family and ate with it. A hired worker or a visitor was not. A daughter who married out ate at her husband's table. If she lost her husband and came home childless, she was taken back in, ‘as in her youth’. Her father's table was open to her again.

The mention of a slave in verse 11 belongs to the world of ancient slavery, which these notes do not defend. The notes on chapter 25 face that subject.

Behind the detail is one concern, stated at the start: that God's name should not be ‘profaned’, treated as common. Holy things handled carelessly teach people that God may be handled carelessly.
passages.later:
The priests' right to this food rested on God's word to Aaron: “I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites” (Numbers 18:20).

When David was a fugitive, a priest gave him holy bread for his hungry men (1 Samuel 21:6). Jesus recalled it when his disciples were accused over the Sabbath, and asked, “Have you never read what David did when he and his companions were hungry and in need?” (Mark 2:25).
passages.asks: A daughter who had lost everything could come home and eat at her father's table as she did when she was young. Ask who has come back to your family or your church after a hard time, and whether there is a place at the table for them. And ask what holy thing you have begun to handle as if it were ordinary.

passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to the priests and to all Israel. Anyone, Israelite or foreign resident, who brings a burnt offering “must offer an unblemished male from the cattle, sheep, or goats in order for it to be accepted on your behalf” (verse 19). “You must not present anything with a defect, because it will not be accepted on your behalf” (verse 20).

An animal that is blind, injured or maimed, or that has sores, is not to be put on the altar (verse 22). An animal with a stunted limb may be given as a freewill offering, but not to keep a vow (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
This passage is for everyone, since everyone brought offerings.

The rule is simple, and the temptation it guards against is as old as worship. A farmer has a fine animal and a poor one. It is easy to keep the best and give God the one that would have fetched nothing at market. The law forbids it. What is given to God is to be whole.

The problem here is not poverty. Leviticus has made room for the poor again and again, with birds and with flour. The problem is contempt: having something good and choosing to give God the leftovers.

The word that runs through the passage is ‘accepted’. An offering is a gift to a person, and a gift shows what the giver thinks of the one who receives it.

The list of defects is close to the list in chapter 21 for priests who served at the altar. Offering and priest together were to be a sign of wholeness. As the note on that chapter says, that was a rule about a sign at the altar. It is not a statement about the worth of any person or any creature.

One small allowance shows the spirit of the law. An animal with a stunted limb could be given as a free gift. It could not be used to pay a vow, a promise already made. A person may give God a small thing freely. He may not pay what he owes with less than he promised.
passages.later:
Centuries later the prophet Malachi accused the priests of his day of allowing exactly this: “When you offer blind animals for sacrifice, is it not wrong?” He adds, “Try offering them to your governor” (Malachi 1:8).

King David refused to give God what cost him nothing. Offered a threshing floor and oxen as a gift, he said, “I insist on paying a price, for I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24).

The New Testament uses this chapter's word of Christ, who “offered Himself unblemished to God” (Hebrews 9:14). And Paul asks believers to give themselves: “offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12:1).
passages.asks: The law would not let people give God what they did not want themselves. Ask what God gets from you: your best hours and first thought, or what is left when everything else is done. And ask whether what you give to others in need is what you would be glad to receive.

passages.t: Mother and young, and the holy name
passages.happening:
“When an ox, a sheep, or a goat is born, it must remain with its mother for seven days” (verse 27). Only from the eighth day may it be offered. “But you must not slaughter an ox or a sheep on the same day as its young” (verse 28).

A thank offering must be eaten the same day (verses 29-30).

Then the close: “You must not profane My holy name. I must be acknowledged as holy among the Israelites. I am the LORD who sanctifies you, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. I am the LORD” (verses 32-33).
passages.hearers:
Two small laws about animals come first. A newborn stays with its mother for a week. And a mother and her young are not to be killed on the same day.

The text gives no reason. Jewish and Christian readers have long seen in these laws a lesson in compassion toward animals. Others read them mainly as keeping a line between life and death. Either way, the law sets a limit on what people may do with the creatures in their power, even on the way to the altar.

Then the last verses gather up everything since chapter 17. Three things are said.

God's name is not to be profaned. To profane is to treat as common what is holy. Israel's whole way of life either honors God's name before the watching world or cheapens it.

God is the one who makes holy: ‘I am the LORD who sanctifies you’. The demand rests on a gift.

And it all goes back to the rescue: ‘who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God’. Israel is asked to be holy because it has been set free and belongs to the one who freed it.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy has a law in the same spirit about a bird's nest: “You may take the young, but be sure to let the mother go” (Deuteronomy 22:7). Proverbs says, “A righteous man regards the life of his animal” (Proverbs 12:10).

Through Ezekiel God speaks of his name profaned among the nations by his own people, and promises, “I will show the holiness of My great name” (Ezekiel 36:23).

The concern of verse 32 stands at the head of the prayer Jesus taught: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name” (Matthew 6:9). To hallow is to treat as holy.
passages.asks: God's name was honored or cheapened by how his people lived. Ask what people who know you would conclude about God from the way you live. And ask how you treat the creatures in your power, the animals you keep or eat, and what kindness toward them would look like.
